extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, artists, and readers interested in aesthetic principles and the artistic life
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and artistic principles from Oscar Wilde's De Profundis about how art and the artistic life should be lived and crafted — guidance on imagination, intensity, originality, sympathy, craft, and the relation of art to conduct and nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live completely for the moment
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates rejecting mechanical tithing of days and instead 'living completely for the moment' so that 'every moment should be beautiful' and the soul be ready for the coming of the bridegroom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wilde contrasts routine duty (tithing mint and rue) with the artist's duty to make moments beautiful; example: Mary Magdalen breaking the alabaster vase to create one beautiful moment. Anti-pattern: rigid, utilitarian scheduling that sacrifices immediacy and beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as the world of light
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination 'is the world of light' and 'the world is made by it'; it is a manifestation of love and distinguishes human beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate art by its imaginative power to create luminous modes of life. Guidance: prioritize works that reveal imaginative insight; anti-pattern is work that the world cannot understand because it lacks imaginative manifestation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the sinner and suffering as sources of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ 'seems to have always loved the sinner as being the nearest possible approach to the perfection of man'—sin and suffering can be 'beautiful holy things and modes of perfection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artistic sympathy should attend to flawed, suffering characters and find beauty in their moments; avoid purely moralistic impulses to tidy or reform such figures into dull respectability (e.g., converting an interesting thief into a tedious honest man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moment of repentance/creation can redeem the past
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'moment of repentance is the moment of initiation' and can 'alter one's past'—transforming past shame into something 'beautiful and holy' by a present act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative and character work, foreground transformative moments that reframe a character's history; craft scenes where an instant of insight or remorse reframes prior events rather than simply moralizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as presence rather than didactic teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: Christ 'does not really teach one anything, but by being brought into his presence one becomes something.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer art that effects change through atmosphere, presence, and example rather than explicit moralizing lectures. Anti-pattern: works that tell the reader what to think instead of evoking it through experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic life embraces dynamic forces, not mechanical aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between mechanical people who 'know where they are going' and those driven by dynamic forces who 'never know where they are going'; artists should welcome uncertainty and dynamic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an artistic life (or work) by its openness to unpredictability and transformation; avoid characters or authors narrowly focused on social rank, office, or utilitarian goals that kill dynamism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know oneself but accept the unknowability of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'to know oneself' is a first achievement, 'to recognise that the soul of a man is unknowable, is the ultimate achievement of wisdom.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good art acknowledges self-knowledge but also leaves room for mystery; avoid exhaustive psychological explanation that removes mystery and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intensity over width in modern art
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Not width but intensity is the true aim of modern art. We are no longer in art concerned with the type. It is with the exception that we have to do.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize concentrated, intense focus and singular passions over broad, encyclopedic scope; craft work that pursues exceptional moments and deep feeling rather than comprehensive types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality: 'Art only begins where Imitation ends'
rubrics_metrics.description: Art must transcend mere imitation; originality marks the start of true art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value novelty and personal voice; works that simply replicate established forms or manners should be seen as imitation, not art. Encourage risk and departure from formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression is necessary; art must be an authentic utterance
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Expression is as necessary to me as leaf and blossoms are to the black branches...’ — art must be a genuine expression of self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works by their expressive force and authenticity; anti-patterns include technically competent pieces that lack authentic emotional or visionary expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft elements to pursue (cadence, memory, architectural order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde lists concrete craft aims: 'fuller memory of words perhaps, of richer cadences, of more curious effects, of simpler architectural order, of some aesthetic quality at any rate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical checklist for stylistic improvement: cultivate memorable diction, richer rhythmic cadences, inventive effects, and clearer structural order. These are criteria for revision and evaluation of prose/poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow plaintive, discontented undertones (the 'cry of Marsyas')
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern art often carries 'the cry of Marsyas'—bitter in Baudelaire, sweet in Lamartine, mystic in Verlaine; a deferred, plaintive voice is valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't suppress discontent or lament in art; the undertone of pain can be an emblem of depth. Guidance: use tonal subtlety—bitterness, plaint, mysticism—to enrich work rather than flattening it into mere prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid philistinism: recognise and foster dynamic force
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Philistine' is described as one who 'upholds and aids the heavy, cumbrous, blind, mechanical forces of society' and 'does not recognise dynamic force when he meets it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a critic or creator, resist audiences and institutions that valorize mechanical conformity over dynamic innovation. Antipattern: celebrating safe, conventional work because it fits social machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use danger and transgressive material for artistic stimulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde defends 'entertaining at dinner the evil things of life' because 'from the point of view through which I...approach them they were delightfully suggestive and stimulating. The danger was half the excitement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transgressive or dangerous subject matter can generate creative energy and suggestiveness—use with artistic intent rather than sensationalism. Beware of moralizing or flattening such material into mere shock value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorrow reveals soul; art should elicit pity, not scorn
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Behind sorrow there is always a soul... to mock at a soul in pain is a dreadful thing.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray sorrow with empathy and depth. Evaluate character portrayals by their capacity to make readers feel pity and understanding, not scorn or ridicule. Anti-pattern: treating suffering as comic spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek elemental directness: art should deal directly with things
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde contrasts 'our art... of the moon and plays with shadows' with 'Greek art... of the sun and deals directly with things,' advocating a return to elemental forces that purify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity, direct engagement with elemental realities (nature, body, simple acts) over excessive artifice or abstruse symbolism. Use sensory, immediate detail that serves lived experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek the Mystical in Art, Life, and Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde declares a desire for 'The Mystical in Art, the Mystical in Life, the Mystical in Nature' and to harmonise with a spirit behind painted forms and shapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should aim beyond surface description toward evoking a deeper hidden spirit; favor works that gesture toward transcendence or a unifying mystery rather than mere surface prettiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain individualism and self-reliance in the artistic life
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde argues he must be 'far more of an individualist than ever I was... get far more out of myself... and ask far less of the world' and criticises appealing to society for help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists should cultivate self-reliance and personal integrity, avoiding dependence on social approval or legal protection. Anti-pattern: creating work primarily to curry favor or to solicit societal leniency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match the scale of emotion to the artist's capacity ('great passions are for the great of soul')
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Great passions are for the great of soul, and great events can be seen only by those who are on a level with them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting monumental passions or events, ensure the representation is commensurate with the artist's insight and capacity; avoid grand themes handled by voices unsuited to their scale (which yields shallow or comic effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and accept literary 'types' and fixed characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Wilde praises Shakespeare's Rosencrantz and Guildenstern as immortal types—'They are types fixed for all time'—arguing some characters belong out of their sphere and should be appreciated as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In characterization, some types are enduring and may be intentionally limited or satiric; accept archetypal figures as valid artistic choices rather than flaws. Evaluate such characters by how well they serve thematic purpose.
